newsitem.title: USA: News conference set in tobacco settlement - source.
newsitem.headline: News conference set in tobacco settlement - source.

text.p: A news conference is set for 1600 EST (2100 GMT ) Thursday in Washington to announce a settlement between Liggett Group and a large group of state attorneys general, a source close to talks said.

Terms of the settlement are expected to include Liggett's agreement to turn over potentially damaging evidence against the tobacco industry and to include warnings on cigarette packages that smoking is addictive.
If the warning is included, it would mark the first time a cigarette company admits that nicotine is addictive.
Attorneys general have been meeting in Washington since Tuesday night to iron out a deal that would include all 22 states suing the industry to recoup health-care costs of smokers.

Scott Harshbarger, the Massachusetts attorney general, would not confirm that the deal was final but told reporters at a briefing on the White House lawn that terms of the pact under consideration would include the turning-over of documents.

"This, were it to be finalized, would be the first time the stone wall has been breached, that evidence is actually being made available from the companies themselves," he said. Harshbarger, who is president of the National Association of Attorneys General, which is meeting in Washington this week, said he was making comments on his own and his views did not reflect those of the association.
He said that if the terms under consideration were met, "it will be one of the most important breakthroughs in the battle against big tobacco and the tobacco wars we have seen."

"This settlement will produce information that indicates that major tobacco companies were fully aware that the product they were selling is addictive, that the product they were selling had great impact on public health in terms of disease and lung cancer and that there was a targeting ...of young people as a major way to try to addict the next generation of adults," he said.
Harshbarger said the evidence that may be turned over could be used in the numerous lawsuits against the tobacco industry.
"This is a very significant victory we believe," he said.
